newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: No crisis from crashed Kazakh bank, say bankers.
newsitem.headline: No crisis from crashed Kazakh bank, say bankers.

text.p: The crash of Kazakhstan's AO KRAMDS Bank, the first commercial bank founded in the Central Asian republic and one of the largest, will not spark a banking crisis, banking sources said on Monday.
"This won't lead to a banking crisis," said a Western banking source based in the Kazakh capital Almaty. "KRAMDS was not heavily exposed on the interbank market," he said.
The National Bank of Kazakhstan (central bank) announced on Monday it had withdrawn KRAMDS Bank's licence, saying it could not meet its obligations.

"KRAMDS Bank has gone into liquidation because of its negative assets, which at September 1 were around minus 2.12 billion tenge ($30 million), and its inability to meet its obligations," Grigory Marchenko, deputy chairman of the National Bank, told a news conference.
There was no immediate comment from KRAMDS Bank.
A crowd of worried depositors gathered outside the modern glass and steel headquarters on Monday morning in the centre of Almaty.
"They (KRAMDS) didn't warn us and they acted like looters," said Irina Shershova, 62, standing in the crowd.
She put 120,000 Kazakh tenge (about $1,700) in the bank hoping to earn annual interest of 27 percent. "This is the last money we have," she said.
In neighbouring Russia, the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange suspended trading on Monday in the Kazakh currency, the tenge, on the news KRAMDS had had its licence withdrawn.

"This was an overreaction, nearly everyone knew this was coming," said a financial analyst in Almaty. "I think the national bank did the right thing. It shows it will only come to the aid of a small number of (healthy) banks," he said.
KRAMDS Bank was founded in 1989 and was said by the banking community to be highly active in Kazakhstan's nascent foreign exchange and debt markets.
In July, the National Bank of Kazakhstan warned the former Soviet republic's 102 struggling banks they had to bring capital ratios up to global standards or face closure.
"It's their choice to die immediately or sometime later," Marchenko said in an interview last July.
KRAMDS is around the 30th bank to be closed this year but one of the biggest names.
